sandhi.type: visarga sandhi; no change; final m before a vowel
sandhi.note: -aḥ before the voiced v becomes -o; the t of वेगात् stays unvoiced before kh; the m of खम् is pronounced with the following u.
The final k stays unvoiced before k; the Gita Press writes the two words together.

samasa.literal: by the enemy of the beasts
by a stroke of the hand
samasa.sense: with a swipe of the paw

morph.note: Two absolutives with the same root and opposite prefixes — उत्पत्य ‘flying up’, निपत्य ‘coming down’ — give the arc of the lion’s spring.
Passive construction: the head is the subject (शिरः, neuter, hence कृतम्) and the lion the agent in the instrumental (मृगारिणा). पृथक् कृ ‘to make separate, sever’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः मृगारिणा वेगात् खम् उत्पत्य निपत्य च करप्रहारेण चामरस्य शिरः पृथक् कृतम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence: agent (मृगारिणा) with two absolutives, instrument (करप्रहारेण), subject (शिरः) and the participle कृतम् as verb.
mantras.lit: Then, by the enemy of beasts, having leapt with speed into the sky and come down, with a blow of the paw, the head of Cāmara was made separate.
mantras.tr: Then the lion sprang swiftly into the air and, coming down, struck off Cāmara’s head with a blow of its paw.
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit is passive (‘Cāmara’s head was severed by the lion’); the translation makes it active.

comm.t: The lion, not the Goddess, kills Cāmara. Her mount fights as her ally, as it did at 2.51–52, where it ranged through the asura army like fire through a forest.

samasa.vigraha: शिलाः च वृक्षाः च शिलावृक्षाः (itaretara dvandva); शिलावृक्षाः आदयः येषां तैः
samasa.literal: by (things) of which rocks and trees are the first
samasa.sense: with boulders, trees and other such missiles

samasa.vigraha: दन्ताः च मुष्टयः च तलाः च, तैः
samasa.literal: by teeth and fists and palms
samasa.sense: biting, punching and slapping — bare-handed combat

morph.note: Past participle of the causative (नि + पातय- + त): ‘made to fall’, i.e. struck down. Contrast निपतिता ‘fallen’ (3.13), from the simple verb.
Passive participle as the verb, with the agent in the instrumental (देव्या). The agent of निपातितः in the second line is not restated; the nearest is देव्या.

mantras.anvaya: रणे देव्या शिलावृक्षादिभिः उदग्रः च हतः, दन्तमुष्टितलैः च एव करालः च निपातितः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two passive clauses on one pattern: instrument + subject + participle. देव्या, stated in the first, is understood in the second.
mantras.lit: And Udagra was slain in battle by the Goddess with rocks, trees and the like; and Karāla too was struck down with teeth, fists and palms.
mantras.tr: Udagra was slain in battle by the Goddess with boulders, trees and the like; and Karāla was felled with teeth, fists and blows of the open hand.

comm.t: Two more generals fall. Udagra was named at 2.41 (उदग्राख्यो महासुरः). The weapons are those of close, improvised combat — rocks, trees, teeth, fists — unlike the arrows and spears so far.

The text names only देव्या as agent. Rocks, trees and teeth are also the weapons of her lion and of the gaṇas born from her breath (2.52–53), who fight as extensions of her; the Sanskrit itself does not say whose hands they were.

sandhi.note: a + u → o. Inside the name, उद् + हत → उद्धत: h after a stop becomes its aspirate (झयो होऽन्यतरस्याम्, 8.4.62).
Visarga before t becomes s; ā + a → ā.

samasa.literal: by the fallings of the mace

morph.note: Periphrastic perfect of the curādi (class 10) root √चूर्ण् (stem चूर्णय-), formed like a causative: चूर्णय + आम् + आस. ‘Made into powder’ (चूर्ण).
Past participle of √क्रुध्: dh + t → ddh (क्रुध् + त → क्रुद्ध). Active in sense: ‘angered’.

mantras.anvaya: क्रुद्धा देवी गदापातैः उद्धतं च चूर्णयामास, भिन्दिपालेन वाष्कलं, बाणैः ताम्रं तथा अन्धकं (जघान)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete. The second lists three more accusatives, each with its weapon; their verb is not stated, and जघान in 3.19 (or चूर्णयामास, extended) governs them.
mantras.lit: The Goddess, enraged, crushed Uddhata with blows of the mace; Bāṣkala with a bhindipāla, Tāmra and likewise Andhaka with arrows.
mantras.tr: In her fury the Goddess crushed Uddhata with her mace; Bāṣkala she struck down with a javelin, and Tāmra and Andhaka with her arrows.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Struck down’ is supplied for the second line, which has no verb of its own.

comm.t: A catalogue of deaths: each general is named with the weapon that kills him. The bhindipāla is among the weapons of the asuras at 2.47 and of the gaṇas at 2.53.

Of the names, Bāṣkala appears among the commanders at 2.43; Uddhata, Tāmra and Andhaka are named here for the first time. उद्धतम् could be taken as an adjective (‘the arrogant one’), but the list of names around it favours a proper name.

samasa.literal: by that which has three points

morph.note: Perfect of √हन् (see 3.4). Its objects are the three names of this verse — and, by the usual reading, the accusatives left without a verb in 3.18.

mantras.anvaya: त्रिनेत्रा परमेश्वरी च त्रिशूलेन उग्रास्यम् उग्रवीर्यं च तथा एव च महाहनुं जघान।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (परमेश्वरी with the epithet त्रिनेत्रा), instrument (त्रिशूलेन), three objects and the verb जघान.
mantras.lit: And the three-eyed Supreme Sovereign slew with the trident Ugrāsya and Ugravīrya, and likewise Mahāhanu.
mantras.tr: And with her trident the three-eyed Supreme Goddess slew Ugrāsya, Ugravīrya and Mahāhanu.

comm.t: Three more generals fall to the trident. The narrator varies her names through the battle — Ambikā (3.2, 3.12), Bhadrakālī (3.9), Devī — and here Trinetrā, ‘the three-eyed’, and Parameśvarī, ‘Supreme Sovereign’, the title Brahmā gave her in his hymn (1.82).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same title as name 396, परमेश्वरी. The shared name reflects a common Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.
